description.purpose: The single durable surface of the hive: the three-level memory ladder (episodes -> facts/entities/edges -> beliefs) with bi-temporal validity, plus the embedding generations, the three identity dimensions of a fact (canonical_subject + canonical_predicate + canonical_claim, each with its own store-owned alias table and its own refusal log), the judged cardinality of a relation (predicate_cardinality) and the four machine tables the lanes keep their state in (pending_extraction, consolidation_log, recall_scratch, scratch). Every durable row also carries WHO may be told about it: `episodes` hold the participant set of the turn (plus who spoke and in which channel), `facts` and `entity_edges` inherit it from their episode, and `beliefs`/`skills` carry the intersection of their sources' (#244). `entities` deliberately carries none -- an entity is reached through edges and facts, and those are filtered.
description.use_when: Every lane of the hive writes and reads here; no cell keeps private state (code cells have none by design).
description.not_in_scope: No joins and no aggregates -- the op dispatcher has neither. The graph and vector legs DO run here (`traverse` and `similar` are shipped store ops), which is the reason the recall fusion is store work and not a walk in a script. Nothing is ever deleted: supersession sets expired_at + superseded_by, belief retraction sets active=0. FTS indexes exist only for tables declared in params.schema — a table created at runtime via create_table cannot carry one. Alias resolution is ONE hop and never transitive: whoever writes an alias writes it already resolved. alias_candidates only PROPOSES pairs; nothing in the store ever merges two entities on similarity. reject_pair records a refusal, it never touches a fact.
description.emits_meaning: messages[]: one tool_result per op; select and search return the projected row array as JSON text, search adds a bm25 `rank` per row (smaller is better). hop.operation drives the lane state machines, hop.rows_affected carries the RMW guard signal (a guarded update that affected 0 rows means another worker won), hop.error_code surfaces SQL failures as normal results.
description.consumes_meaning: messages[]: tool_call turns with store-native args {operation, table, ...}; select and search need an explicit columns array. where accepts comparison operators (eq/neq/lt/lte/gt/gte/in/is_null/or_null) besides bare equality, plus order_by, limit and (select only) distinct — the last one answers a SET question at the store, so a caller that wants the axes a table carries rather than its rows pays for the axes; under distinct every order_by column has to be projected, else the prefix a limit returns would not be defined. set_alias, reject_pair, canonicalize and alias_candidates name the BOUND table (facts), never the alias table — the binding in params.canonical resolves the rest; a table with two bindings needs `column` (the binding's SOURCE column) to say which dimension is meant, and canonicalize without it re-derives every dimension. The lane that a reply belongs to is carried by context.store_origin ('episode' | 'extract' | 'inline' | 'recall' | 'dream'), promoted by the edge that sent the op.
examples: {operation: insert, table: episodes, row: {...}} -> tool_result 'ok', hop {operation: 'insert', rows_affected: 1}

predicate identity: facts.predicate is what was written, facts.canonical_predicate is what it MEANS — store-owned, derived on every write from predicate_aliases, and the only column the keyword / axis / chain legs consume

entity identity: facts.canonical_subject is the same mechanism one dimension over, plus normalisation (Unicode composition, case fold, whitespace collapse) -- two spellings equal after it are ONE axis at mint time, with no alias and no judgement

statement identity: facts.canonical_claim is the same mechanism a third dimension over, and it is what makes the SUPERSESSION unit the statement (canonical_subject, canonical_predicate, canonical_claim) while the axis stays the retrieval grouping -- byte identity of the claim is the day-one canonical value, judged claim aliases are a later package

closure attribution: facts.closure_source names WHO closed a statement (a judgement), and it is empty on a closure the chain re-derives by itself (a later assertion of the same statement). An unattributed closure is withdrawn by the next re-derive, which is the revert path for judgements

run books: consolidation_log carries what one night COST -- llm_calls counts the model calls of that run and tokens_prompt/tokens_completion sum what those replies reported. NULL in a token column means 'no reply reported usage', never 'nothing was spent'

cardinality: predicate_cardinality holds one judged verdict per canonical predicate (single | multi) with the source that decided it, and the read stack is seed > judged > learned-with-session-guard. The seed list is authority and never becomes a row, so a predicate ON that list carrying a judged row is a contradiction the write path refuses rather than a precedence the reader has to untangle. The revert is a delete on the source of one night

{operation: set_alias, table: facts, column: 'predicate', alias: 'Lieblingseditor', canonical: 'favorite_editor'} -> upsert into predicate_aliases; then {operation: canonicalize, table: facts} pulls BOTH derived columns, rows_affected = identities that MOVED

{operation: alias_candidates, table: facts, column: 'subject', limit: 20, min_score: 0.5} -> [{left, right, score}] sorted best first: the nightly GC's feed of entity pairs that MIGHT be the same, pairs it already settled excluded

{operation: reject_pair, table: facts, column: 'subject', left: 'robin', right: 'robyn'} -> upsert into subject_rejected_pairs: the GC judged them DIFFERENT, so the feed stops proposing them; the pair is unordered and the revert is a delete on that table
revert: {operation: delete, table: predicate_aliases, where: {alias: '...'}} + canonicalize -> every row falls back onto its untouched original
as-of query: {operation: select, table: facts, columns: [...], where: {valid_from: {lte: T}, valid_until: {or_null: {gt: T}}}} -> only the facts true at T

{operation: update, table: pending_extraction, set: {status: 'claimed', batch_id: 'b1', claimed_at: '2026-08-15T09:00:00.000000Z'}, where: {status: 'pending'}} -> hop.rows_affected > 0 means this worker owns the batch, and claimed_at is when it started owning it (GH #72: a recovery sweep reclaims a claim only after its lease has run out)
NULL means open: facts.expired_at NULL = live, facts.valid_until NULL = currently true, embeddings.blob NULL = not embedded yet (queued via status)
scratch: the join-less store cannot return two result sets at once, so a lane that must diff set A against set B parks both under one key and reads them back in a single select
